# Epilogue: Guardian of the Shadows

Three months later.

The morning sun broke over the craggy coastline of mid-coast Maine, painting the Atlantic waters in brilliant shades of amber, copper, and sapphire. A gentle salt breeze drifted through the towering white pines, carrying the sweet aroma of wild blueberries and coastal spruce.

On the wrap-around cedar porch of a secluded, beautiful two-story craftsman home perched on the bluff, Victor stood with a steaming mug of black coffee in his hands.

He wore a comfortable flannel shirt, faded denim jeans, and work boots. The bruises that had covered his body in Scotland were long gone, replaced by a lean, hardened athletic grace that made him look ten years younger than his thirty-eight years.

Down on the manicured lawn overlooking the rocky beach, the sound of joyous, uninhibited laughter floated up to the porch.

Jessica was kneeling in the grass, laughing as eight-year-old Lucas and six-year-old Emma chased a boisterous golden retriever puppy across the lawn. The puppy tumbled over Lucas's sneakers, sending both boy and dog rolling into the clover in a tangle of giggles and wagging tail. Jessica looked up toward the porch, her long auburn hair catching the sunlight, and caught Victor's gaze. She blew him a kiss, her eyes radiant with the deep, uninterrupted peace they had fought so hard to reclaim.

The Order had kept its word.

The estate had been purchased through a legitimate historical preservation trust, fully funded, completely private, and secured beneath layers of legal and physical protection that no mortal agency could penetrate. A mile down the private access road, two trusted Franciscan field sentinels lived in a quiet cottage, while deep in the surrounding pine forest, a mated pair of wolves from the Maine coastal clan kept silent, unseen vigil over the property.

Victor took a sip of coffee, feeling the warm ceramic mug against his palms.

His smartphone buzzed softly on the cedar railing.

Victor picked it up. An encrypted text message flashed across the display from a private Vatican routing node:

*[08:14 EST] — Archbishop Talbot: Mediterranean transit completed without incident. The Milanese tribunal has sentenced Mercer to perpetual monastic sequestration. The Argentum storage facility in Zurich has been dismantled and converted to a relic preservation archive. The Church remembers its vow. Peace be upon your house, Victor.*

A second notification chimed immediately after, originating from a secure satellite link in the Virginia Blue Ridge:

*[08:16 EST] — Sowain: The Rockville pack has completed autumn integration. Rebecca has assumed leadership of the eastern scouts. We have established diplomatic contact with the Adirondack council; they have agreed to the terms of the New Covenant without hesitation. Marcus sends his regards. Enjoy the salt air, nephew. The forest is quiet.*

Victor smiled, sliding the phone back into his pocket.

He turned and walked through the sliding screen door into his private study.

The room was warm and quiet, lined with oak bookshelves and nautical charts of the Maine coast. Resting upon a velvet-lined display stand atop an antique mahogany sideboard was the iron-banded chest of Castile.

Inside the open case, resting on crimson silk, lay *Lobera* and the Jamestown dagger.

The celestial steel lay completely still, its gold scripture glowing with a faint, almost imperceptible sapphire luminescence that pulsed in steady cadence with Victor's breath. It was no longer a weapon of terror; it was a beacon of guardianship.

From the hallway, light footsteps padded across the hardwood floor.

Emma slipped into the study, holding a half-eaten blueberry muffin, her bright blue eyes looking curiously at the sword, then up at her father.

"Daddy?" she asked, tugging on his flannel sleeve. "Are you going to come play with Duke on the beach? Lucas says the dog found a hermit crab!"

Victor knelt down, wrapping his strong arm around his daughter and kissing the top of her head. "I wouldn't miss it for the world, sweetheart."

He glanced once more at the ancient blade of Saint Ferdinand.

The shadows would always exist in the corners of the world. Men would still fear the dark, and monsters would still occasionally test the perimeter. But as long as the bloodline endured, and as long as the Arbiter drew breath, the line would hold.

Victor took his daughter's hand, walked out into the morning sunlight, and closed the door behind him.

---
